  1. How to Source and Evaluate Uplistings

  2. Putting It Together - A Real Life Trade

Uplistings.

There’s tremendous opportunity in monitoring new NYSE and Nasdaq listings, but not in the way you think. The real edge isn’t in red-hot IPOs at sky-high valuations, but rather “graduates” from the Over-The-Counter Market; forgotten, discarded businesses with rapidly inflecting prospects who regain enough fundamental footing to be admitted to the “big leagues”. If conducted properly, an exchange uplisting can serve as a massive catalyst, drawing Equity Research attention, enabling Index Inclusion, and ultimately opening the floodgates to Institutional Capital.

Some of the most extraordinary winners of 2024 and 2025 have been uplistings as the AI / Electrification Boom resuscitates businesses back to life.

Power Solutions, for example, is up nearly 199% since its uplisting and more than 40x its April 2024 low of $2.00. After fending off near bankruptcy, Power Solutions took advantage of heightened AI demand for power systems and soaring revenues and profits grew shareholder’s equity from just $3 Million at the end of 2023 to $65 Million at the end of 2024. Given its significantly improved financial footing, Power Solutions was able to re-list on Nasdaq in December 2024, nearly 7 years after it was first delisted in April 2017.

The flood of institutional capital has continued. After a brief drop to $20, the stock has since soared to $88; it is now an “AI Darling” and a Russell 2000 component.

Talen Energy (TLN) is a similar story. After emerging from bankruptcy in May of 2023, the stock languished on the Over-The-Counter market despite rapidly improving fundamentals as a reuslt of skyrocketing power pricing. Earnings and Cash Flow surged as the company reduced its share count through a highly unusual tender offer in June 2024 at $116. It was uplisted to the Nasdaq in July, becoming “accessible” to Institutional Investors who were precluded from trading OTC names. It is up 183% since then.

It’s incredibly easy to find uplistings before they occur. All you need to do is the control-F equivalent for “Uplisting” on Edgar - use its full-text search functionality. In fact, I’ve already done the work for you, just click here.

Nearly every company announces its intention to uplist months in advance; I check this link daily to maintain a list of uplistings in progress that I am interested in, as well as those that will soon be effective.

Checking daily might be a pain, but it is a great way to spot opportunities before others.

An uplisting itself isn’t a sure sign of success. You could run through the value trade checklist, but there is an even easier way to filter out the potential winners from the garbage. Ask yourself a very simply question, why is this company uplisting?

If the uplisting is pre-revenue company, in a disreputable industry, or simply a shell game like Bitmine Inversion Technologies becoming a crypto treasury company, it’s an immediate red flag. Stay away from companies who have uplisted for the purpose of raising additional capital by selling fresh shares. Many times a reverse-merger uplisting is simply a way to avoid the regulatory scrutiny of an IPO. While you might be able to win, in general you will serve as someone’s exit liquidity.

Instead, focus on companies that are already profitable, growing, and have a strong or inflecting story. Chances are the uplisting is intended to boost visibility and provide long-term holders with additional value and improved liquidity. Pay special attention to names that are buying back shares into the uplisting, like Talen Energy did, this is a strong signal.

While not all uplistings are success stories, incorporating a simple once-a-week check of Edgar is a great way to source fresh ideas, provided you are a skilled, active, investor. Uplistings are a prime hunting ground to identify and get in on inflecting businesses, before Institutional Investors can.

Here’s one that has caught my eye.

Putting It Together - A Real Life Trade

Acorn Energy ($ACFN) is a Hardware-as-a-Service business specializing in advanced generator monitoring. Its proprietary Omnimetrix Trueguard Pro platform enables large commercial clients and residential generator dealers to remotely monitor their fleets via convenient web and mobile apps. Trueguard Pro hardware is easy to install and universally compatible. It plugs directly into generator circuit boards, giving clients full remote control and relaying critical information like battery voltage, fuel levels, temperature, and oil pressure via cellular or satellite.

The product is a huge value add. Not only does Trueguard add value to the generators themselves by identifying critical issues to be fixed before they cause total generator failure, Trueguard significantly reduces recurring service costs as dealers and commercial clients are able to identify faulty components without an initial inspection, enabling them to source parts and perform a fixes in one trip.

The value provided by Trueguard is especially immense when deployed in remote locations. In June 2024, a major US Cell Provider selected Omnimetrix to provide remote monitoring on backup generators at 5,000 cell tower sites. It’s not hard to understand why a $500 - $750 monitor is an excellent deal when the cost to even send a repair team for an initial inspection can be as high as $5,000.

Acorn’s real financial gem, however, is not the hardware it sells but rather the high margin, annual recurring revenue driven by the monitoring software it sells with the hardware. Although the output data from the hardware monitors comes in an open format, pretty much every customer opts to use Omnimetrix’s monitoring software platform which provides early detection, text / email alerts, and remote control for an extremely low price. After all, would anyone really gripe about a $15 - $25 monthly monitoring fee for a $30,000 generator? Does a guy with a $300,000 vintage Mercedes add an extra 15-minutes in parking so his car isn’t towed and scratched? Of course, they want to protect their investment.

Revenue increased 3% in 2022, 15% in 2023, 35% in 2024, and is guided for a further 20% increase this year as a result of the $5 Million cell contract. A significant chunk of the 2025 increase has been driven by elevated hardware demand as a result of the cell contract (hardware gross margin is 55%), but the main thing I am paying attention to is the sharp inflection in monitoring revenue, given the segment operates at an outstanding 94% gross margin.

Monitoring Revenue was up 5.4% in Q1 and 15% year over year, and is primed for further increases as the company stated during the last earnings call that only 66% of the hardware for the cell contract had been installed, indicating that additional monitoring revenue growth is possible as the remaining units come online.

I think Acorn has substantial pricing power. Unlike Acorn’s direct sales in the commercial market, Acorn does not sell directly in the residential generator market. Instead, generator dealers purchase Acorn’s hardware and offer monitoring and maintenance packages to their clients, using Omnimetrix’s underlying technology. The monitoring / maintenace packages these dealers sell are huge profit sources for them, as a result, Omnimetrix has substantial pricing power as most of their monitoring contracts are renewed on a one or two year basis and cost a fraction of what the dealers are making from their residential customers.

I despise businesses who love to “increase prices in-line with broader inflation” for no reason, but Omnimetrix certainly has that option available to them given the massive value their product provides. Obviously, given monitoring margins are already 94%, they seem to have figured this out.

Before we get into valuation, it’s important to analyze management alignment, credibility, and guidance for the year.

Jan Loeb, the CEO, joined Acorn Energy in 2016 after providing rescue financing to the business. Under his leadership, Acorn has fixed its balance sheet, and cemented its focus on generator monitoring after acquiring an additional 19% of OmniMetrix in 2019 (it now owns 99%, with the initial founder owning the remaining 1%).

He takes a very reasonable salary (given the stock performance) of $330,000 a year, and owns 528,000 shares (21% of the company, $14 Million). Additional Acorn executives own 14%, and Joel Sklar, a former insurance executive and micro cap investors owns 5%. Simply put, the insiders and owners of Acorn are highly incentivized to see the company do well, their ownership dwarfs their compensation.

Prior to rescuing Acorn, Jan was a director, and then lead independent director, of American Pacific Corporation, and presided over a 650% return in the stock before it was acquired by NewMarket. He was also an independent director Golf Trust of America, a golf focused REIT, from 2006 to 2011; the stock doubled before it divested its golf assets and was acquired by a pharmaceutical company in a reverse merger in 2014. Jan is also the Executive Chairman of Novelstem International (NSTM), a rescue situation he became involved in around 2019. The company is now defunct, given the fact the market cap was just $2 Million when he joined and the company’s viability was predicted on an intellectual property claim, I don’t really hold this against him; it was probably doomed from the start. Overall, given his experience as a director at American Pacific Corporation and GolfTrust, as well as his career at Jefferies, Wasserstein, and the management of his own fund, Lead Tide Capital Management, I think it is reasonable to say he knows his way around finance and has a respectable track record.

Mangement’s guidance seems attainble. The company outlined clear plans to uplist earlier this year and the 50% year over year increase in Q1 revenue lends credence to recent guidance for 20% overall revenue growth.

“Uplisting to Nasdaq is an exciting milestone for our employees and other stakeholders. It underscores our transformation from a diversified entity with a history of operating losses to a focused, high-margin, cash-generating growth business. Based on favorable trends driving demand for backup generators and remote monitoring, we believe we can grow our revenue at an average annual rate of 20% or more, over the next three-to-five year period, while bringing approximately 50% of each incremental revenue dollar to the operating profit line. We expect to exceed our 20% growth target in 2025 and believe our Nasdaq listing will support us in continuing to grow and build shareholder value.”

The uplisting was successful, and the company transferred to the Nasdaq last Thursday.

There will likely be a slowdown later this year as hardware shipments related to the cell contract come to an end, yet the 20% revenue guidance was given just a week ago, which implies the company either has a new large contract in the works, or that monitoring revenue is primed to take off.

The company currently trades around 34x my calculated 2025 earnings. Nuts, right? This doesn’t seem anything similar to the 9478 or CGEO value trades.

You’re right.

The potential for Acorn isn’t in its current numbers, but rather, whether the company can continue to execute and add high margin annual recurring revenue through monitoring.

Using my own base assumptions, which are significantly lower than the implied guidance (revenue growth of 13% in 2025, 7% in 2026, and 10% in 2027), Acorn has a path towards $1.37 in EPS by 2027, which would imply an 18x P/E at the current price fo $24.91. Still expensive, but given the high operating margins of annual recurring monitoring revenue, and the niche problem the product solves, I think this is actually not wildly unreasonable.

Using more optimistic projections that are still below company guidance, it appears a path to $1.94 in EPS by 2027 is possible, which would be 12x at the current price of $24.91.

It’s important to note Acorn has more than $60 Million of Federal Net Operating Losses and $16 Million of State Net Operating Losses that can be utilized to minimize taxes. The Net Income figure I computed does not include income taxes, since it is likely that Acorn will not be paying corporate taxes for the foreseeable future.

While Accorn trades at a lofty valuation currently, its possible the company is very cheap on 2027 numbers.

Obviously, there are many risks. The most obvious one is if the major cell provider decides to write its own monitoring software, and doesn’t renew the monitoring contract, although in Acorn’s recent June update they state they “expect recurring monitoring revenue in future years” from the contract, so the risk as this point isn’t too significant.

Acorn has a few competitors who are also brand agnostic, namely Power Telematics. Even if price competition gets extreme, I do not think competition poses an extreme risk to Acorn given their sticky customer base. Even if someone is able to entirely clone their web / mobile app and hardware offering, it’s extremely difficult to get existing customers to switch. Since these monitors requires technicians to install, and many of them are in remote locations, even if a competitor offered monitoring for free, the payback period to purchase hardware and send out an installation team would be decades.

Lastly, there is the possibility generator manufacturers begin providing integrated monitoring on new models, but I don’t think this is to much of a threat as it wouldn’t impact Omnimetrix’s existing operations. Furthermore, there would still be a need for a brand agnostic platform like Omnimetrix, as no operator of a 10,000+ generator fleet would want to handle 8-10 different apps with varying monitoring and control abilities. I think that, in fact, Omnimetrix has an opportunity to work with manufacturers that lack monitoring. Why develop your own product when you can just license Omnimetrix’s existing platform as your own?

The valuation here is rich, but I see potential upside if Acorn Energy is able to deliver on its 20% guided revenue target. The story straightfoward, Acorn delivers a huge value add product and generates significant high margin revenue through its innovative monitoring offerings. It stands to benefit from additional large contracts, growing electrification, potential integration with manufacturers, and is an Internet-Of-Things software provider disguised as a hardware manufacturer. Right now, there is no known institutional ownership, and no equity research coverage.

Naturally, the stock has run from $18 to $24.91 before I was able to publish this piece. I want to be clear, Acorn is not a high conviction trade, it’s a special situation that involves significant speculation. A huge portion of the thesis rests on the company being able to meet its 20% annual revenue growth target. If the company is indeed on track for 20% revenue growth in 2025 however, and monitoring revenues grow a further 5% quarter over quarter, I suspect the story will begin to get out and Institutional Investors will get interested. Given the recent run up, Acorn is no longer a deep value name, but I have initiated a very disciplined, small starter position (less than 0.5% of my portfolio) ahead of the company’s first “big league” earnings call next Thursday. With visibility improving and uplisting opening the door to Institutional Capital, Acorn is a name that should be on your radar.
